title: Test the Spirits; God Is Love
summary: John tells his readers not to believe every spirit but to test them: the Spirit of God confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, while the spirit of the antichrist does not. He then turns to love. God is love, and he showed it by sending his one and only Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. Those who know God love one another, and perfect love drives out fear. No one can love the unseen God while hating the brother he can see.
story: Chapter 3 ended by saying that believers know God remains in them by the Spirit he has given. But many were claiming the Spirit, including those who had left. Chapter 4 therefore begins by showing how to tell the Spirit of God from false spirits, returning to the test of belief. It then gives the letter's most sustained reflection on love, grounded not in human feeling but in God's own nature and his act of sending the Son. Chapter 5 will draw the three tests of belief, love, and obedience together.
historical:
The false prophets of verse 1 are almost certainly the teachers who had left John's community, now spreading their message elsewhere. Early Christianity valued prophecy as a gift of the Spirit, and traveling prophets were common, which made discernment urgent. Paul too told churches to test prophecies (1 Thessalonians 5:20-21), and the Didache, an early church manual, later gave practical tests for prophets, such as whether they asked for money.

The test John gives, confessing that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, points to the likely shape of the opponents' teaching. They seem to have denied that the divine Christ was truly and permanently joined to human flesh, a view later called docetism. Early in the second century, Ignatius of Antioch wrote letters to churches in the same region, including Smyrna and Tralles, warning against teachers who said that Christ only seemed to suffer. John's letter shows the same danger at an earlier stage.
cultural:
In the Greco-Roman world, spirits, oracles, and inspired speech were part of ordinary religious life. People consulted oracles such as the one at Delphi, and ecstatic speech was associated with many cults. The claim to be moved by a spirit carried no automatic authority. John's readers would have understood that not every inspired-sounding voice comes from God.

The statement God is love would also have struck ancient ears as unusual. Greek religion told stories of gods who loved and lusted, but the gods were not love itself, and philosophers tended to describe the highest divine being as unmoved and self-sufficient, not as one who sends his son to die. John does not say that love is God, as if any love were divine. He says that God is love, and then defines love by what God did in sending his Son. The phrase one and only Son (monogenes) also occurs in John's Gospel (John 1:14, 1:18, 3:16), and verse 9 reads almost as a commentary on John 3:16.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-6 set two groups side by side in parallel sentences: the Spirit of God and the spirit of antichrist, those from God and those from the world, the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception. Verses 7-21 form one of the most concentrated passages on love in the Bible; the noun and the verb for love occur in nearly every sentence. The argument moves in a spiral: love is from God, God is love, God showed his love by sending his Son, so we ought to love one another, and in doing so God's love is made complete in us. Twice John says God is love (verses 8 and 16). The final verses return to the test of verse 20, a sharp and memorable contrast between the unseen God and the brother who is seen.

outline.t: Testing the spirits by their confession of Christ
God is love, shown in sending his Son
The Spirit, the confession, and abiding in love

doctrines.note: God is love (verses 8 and 16). Love is not merely something God does but who he is, and Christians have seen here a reflection of the love shared eternally between the Father, the Son, and the Spirit.
Love is defined not by our love for God but by his love for us in sending his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins (verse 10). The cross is where the meaning of love is learned.
The Spirit of God is known by his witness to Jesus Christ come in the flesh. Believers know they remain in God because he has given them his Spirit (verse 13).
Love made complete gives confidence on the day of judgment. Fear has to do with punishment, and the one who knows God's love need not approach judgment in dread (verses 17-18).

words.note: Agape, love, used twelve times in this chapter. In earlier Greek it was a less common word, and the New Testament writers made it their main term for the self-giving love of God. John defines it by action: God sent his Son. It is not first an emotion but a commitment to another's good at cost to oneself.

Monogenes, one and only, or unique. Older translations rendered it only begotten, taking it from words for being born. Most scholars now think it means unique, one of a kind, and it was used of an only child. It stresses that the Son God sent is not one among many but uniquely his own.

Dokimazo, to test or examine, a word used for testing metals to prove whether they were genuine. John tells believers to test the spirits before trusting them. Discernment is not suspicion but loyalty to the truth about Christ.

christ: The chapter shows Christ as the dividing line between truth and error: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is from God (verse 2). It also shows him as the supreme act of God's love. God sent his one and only Son into the world so that we might live through him (verse 9), sent him as the atoning sacrifice for our sins (verse 10), and sent him to be the Savior of the world (verse 14). John writes as one of those who saw and testify to this. The incarnation and the cross belong together: the Son came in the flesh so that in the flesh he could die for sins.

hard.q: If God is love, how can he also judge and punish?
hard.a:
Some readers take verse 8 to mean that a loving God could never condemn anyone, and the tension is real. But the same chapter that says God is love also speaks of the day of judgment (verse 17) and of love expressed in an atoning sacrifice for sins (verse 10), which assumes that sin is serious enough to require one. Most Christian theology has held that God's love and justice are not rivals. Love that did not oppose what destroys the beloved would be indifference, not love, and God's judgment is his settled opposition to evil. The cross shows both at once: God does not overlook sin, and he bears its cost himself.

Christians differ over how final judgment works and what it involves, but John's pastoral point is clear. For those who have come to know God's love, judgment is no longer a thing to dread. Perfect love drives out fear because it rests on what God has done, not on how well we have loved.

questions: John tells his readers to test the spirits. What are the voices around you, inside the church or outside it, that most need testing, and what test would John have you use?
John defines love by God's sending of his Son rather than by our love for God. How does starting there change the way you think about your own love for others?
Which fears in your life have to do with punishment, and what would it look like for God's love to drive them out?
